title: 7 Lightroom Classic 16 Features Worth Learning, Including a New Vectorscope
summary: Lightroom Classic update brings color grading into masks and adds a new vectorscope
detailed: Lightroom Classic released its November update featuring seven key additions including import file-type filtering, color grading within masks, and a new vectorscope.
Terry Vander Heiden reviewed the update, highlighting tools like a Transform panel Projection slider for wide-angle group shots and an AI-powered blemish removal feature.
The update also introduces a Focus Points metadata overlay for wildlife photographers and a Glow tool with various styles that runs inside masks.
These workflow enhancements matter because they reduce the need to switch to Photoshop and streamline repetitive culling and editing tasks.
sentences: Lightroom Classic's November update brings color grading into masks, a vectorscope for checking skin tones, and a projection slider aimed at the stretched people who end up on the edges of wide-angle group shots.
If most of your editing lives in Lightroom Classic, several of these changes cut out trips to Photoshop and long, zoomed-in culling sessions.
Seven features made the list when Terry Vander Heiden walked through the newest release, and the first one sits in the Import dialog, where it's easy to miss.
You can now filter a card by file type before anything comes in.
Click "None," check only raw, and the clips that share the card with your stills drop out of the grid.
Vander Heiden shoots video alongside his raw files and keeps those clips in a separate folder outside the catalog, so unchecking each video thumbnail by hand used to eat time on every import.
He admits he doubted the feature at first and came around after using it.
The bigger change for landscape and wildlife work is that color grading now lives inside masks.
Until this release, the color wheels were global, so you could cool a whole scene or warm it, but splitting the treatment between subject and background took workarounds.
Vander Heiden builds a subject mask on a female elk, adds a linear gradient for the background, and subtracts the subject from that gradient so the cool shift doesn't spill across her back.
He then pushes the background's shadows and midtones toward blue and nudges the elk slightly warmer.
Cool tones recede and warm ones advance, the same effect that turns distant mountains purple.
Having that control per region lets you build depth with color in places where a single global grade would flatten the scene.
For portraits, there's a new vectorscope.
Right-click in the Develop module to show it, and a diagonal line marks the zone where most human skin tones fall.
The cluster on the scope represents the whole image, but you want its bulk sitting on that line.

On Vander Heiden's test portrait, it leaned a little to the left, meaning the skin read too yellow, and the fix turned out to be the tint slider: a little more magenta brought the cluster back onto the line.
Group portraits get their own fix in the Transform panel.
A wide-angle lens stretches whoever stands at the ends of the row, and the new Projection slider pulls those figures back toward natural proportions.

The change is hard to judge side by side, so Vander Heiden stacks the corrected and original versions as layers in Photoshop, aligns them, and toggles the top layer to show how much wider the edge figures looked before.
The new blemish removal sits at the bottom of the Remove tool.
Click Apply, and AI finds and removes blemishes across the image.

A slider dials back how many it removes, a separate natural marks control leaves features such as moles alone unless you push it to 100%, and the Refine button shows every spot Lightroom flagged so you can brush any of them back with Restore.
For portrait shooters, that means clients see cleaned-up images before they ever ask for retouching.
Wildlife shooters get a Focus Points overlay in the Develop module, which reads your camera's metadata to show where it focused.
Going through an hour's worth of pika frames from Yellowstone, he can see at a glance that one landed on the eye and another on the ear after the animal turned its head, without zooming in on each.
Glow, the last of the seven, was already in Camera Raw, but he finds the Lightroom Classic version better.
It works on highlights, offers bloom, diffusion, halation, motion, and streak styles, and runs inside masks.

His demo builds a landscape mask, trims it with a soft subtracted brush, and uses the motion style to send light streaks through a line of trees and onto a road, then subtracts a linear gradient when the effect looks overdone.
He suggests the same approach for city lights or a lit cabin window, since it softens the highlights while the rest of the image stays sharp.
The light streaks build up step by step in the video, from the full-strength effect to the toned-down version.
